extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy, pop culture, and #MeToo/gender issues
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance embedded in an opinion piece about how comedians and public figures respond to #MeToo, and how to judge statements about comedic work (e.g., Nanette) and industry behavior. Focus is on ethical awareness, factual accuracy, and understanding evolving forms of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be an ally; seek to understand victims' perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians and powerful men should try to understand the perspectives of victims and speak up as allies rather than remaining silent or indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes repeated examples (Olivia Munn speaking up alone, the Golden Globes silence) to show that silence is common; it argues that men often don't speak up out of confusion or self-protection, and that this failure to act is problematic. Scoring note: public figures who educate themselves, publicly support accusers, or use their platform to amplify victims rate higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not evaluate or dismiss work you haven't experienced
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid commenting authoritatively about another creator's work when you haven't actually seen it or engaged with it yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights Macdonald saying 'I have never seen the Nanette thing because I never wanted to comment on it' and then criticizing it based on secondhand reports. Anti-pattern: forming and broadcasting judgments based on summaries or hearsay. Better practice: view the work before offering critique, or qualify remarks as preemptive/uninformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect non-traditional forms of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not insist that comedy must be only about producing laughter; accept that comedic expression can include one-person shows and work that foregrounds serious themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macdonald's claim that Gadsby 'is saying that comedy is now not about laughter' is called out as inaccurate; the article defends Nanette as a powerful form that may differ from traditional laugh-driven stand-up. Evaluators should be open to evolving genres and the legitimacy of hybrid or serious comedic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge how privilege shapes perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that white, wealthy, straight, male privilege shapes what people notice and how they interpret industry scandals and marginalized voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece frames Macdonald's obliviousness as an example of privilege that explains why powerful men historically turned a blind eye. When assessing statements or behavior, consider the speaker's social position and how it may limit empathy or awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence in the face of abuse constitutes complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Public silence or refusal to engage with industry-wide problems is interpreted as complicity rather than neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Golden Globes attendees who stayed silent despite dedicating the night to #TimesUp. The article treats failure to speak up as morally significant; evaluators should penalize inaction when public influence could be used to support victims or accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting personal friendships bias judgments about accused individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Being more likely to be friends with an accused person than an accuser can blind people to wrongdoing; evaluators should guard against this bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests a root cause for hesitation to condemn misconduct is friendship networks. Good practice includes seeking objective evidence, listening to accusers, and separating personal loyalties from public moral judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misrepresent others' arguments or facts when criticizing them
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure factual accuracy when summarizing or critiquing another person's work or statements; avoid attributing claims they did not make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macdonald is cited as saying things about Nanette that the show does not say. Anti-pattern: asserting false claims about an artist's intent or content. Guidance: verify quotes and assertions before building critique on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not relegate marginalized creators to marginal categories to minimize them
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dismissing or reclassifying the work of less famous or marginalized creators as 'not real stand-up' to keep them on the fringes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes Macdonald for suggesting Nanette be removed from 'his male-dominated profession and pushed into a more marginalized genre'—presented as an instance of marginalization. Evaluators should resist taxonomy that diminishes marginalized voices and consider whether genre boundaries are being weaponized to exclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be self-aware about social context when making jokes or public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comics and public figures should be aware of changing social norms (e.g., around sexual misconduct) and avoid appearing genuinely confused about basic human interactions or boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cites Seinfeld and Alec Baldwin's bewildered remarks as examples of successful men displaying confusion rather than comedic irony, which undercuts credibility. Good practice: demonstrate awareness of context and the potential real-world effects of casual remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept accountability and the reality of consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that consequences (including job loss) can be a necessary part of accountability for abuse, rather than framing them as evidence of excessive punishment or a lack of forgiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macdonald's comments about victims not having to 'lose everything' are presented as misunderstanding accountability. Evaluators should consider whether public calls for consequences are proportional and aimed at systemic change, and should not reflexively treat consequences as unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning condemnation into a performative contest
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce responses to abuse into a competition about who can express the most disgust or moral superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dana Carvey's remark about 'Are you going to try and top people about how disgusted you are? It’s a competition online' is used to illustrate how online/industry dynamics can trivialize real harms. Evaluators should value sincere, substantive engagement over performative displays of outrage.
